key_terms.meaning: The guarded block of statements Python runs first; if any statement inside it fails, control jumps out to a matching except clause.
The handler that names an exception class and runs only when that class of error is raised inside the matching try.
The block after all except clauses that runs only when the try finished with no exception at all.
The block that always runs, whether the try succeeded, failed, or left through return, break or continue.
The keyword that throws an exception object on purpose, e.g. raise ValueError("bad input").
A ready-made exception class supplied by Python, such as ZeroDivisionError, ValueError, KeyError or FileNotFoundError.
Your own class written as a subclass of Exception so it can be caught by a name that matches your problem.
The instance created when an error occurs; it carries a message and attributes, and is bound to the name in except ... as name.
The value returned by open(); it holds the connection to the file on disk and the methods read, write, seek and close.
The position in the file, in characters (bytes for binary mode), where the next read or write will start; seek moves it, tell reports it.
The second argument to open() that decides the action: 'r' read, 'w' write and truncate, 'a' append, plus 'b' for binary or '+' for both.
A block that closes the file automatically on exit, even if an exception occurs inside, replacing a manual try/finally.
The character that separates fields on one line of a formatted file: a comma in CSV, a tab in TSV.
Python's standard module whose reader and writer objects convert between rows (lists of strings) and delimited lines.
The standard module for folders and the operating system: listdir, mkdir, remove, rename, getcwd, and the os.path helpers.
The list of command-line words that started the program; sys.argv[0] is the script name, the rest are the arguments.
One .py file whose functions, classes and variables are used in another file through import.
A folder of modules containing an __init__.py file, imported as a single dotted name such as college.results.
The test if __name__ == "__main__": that runs code only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported.
A pattern string in a small metalanguage that describes a set of strings, tested or searched with the re module.

takeaways: A try statement lets you name, in advance, the errors you expect and say what to do for each, so the rest of the program keeps running.
Use else for code that should run only on success and finally for cleanup that must run either way.
Every error is an object of a class in the exception hierarchy, so catching a parent class catches all its children.
Write user-defined exceptions as subclasses of Exception so they carry a meaningful name and their own message.
A file object is a handle plus a moving pointer; 'w' truncates, 'a' adds at the end, and the with statement guarantees close.
Read text files line by line in a loop instead of loading a huge file in one go.
CSV and TSV files are plain text tables; the csv module handles quoting and delimiters so you do not split strings by hand.
os manipulates folders and paths, while sys exposes the interpreter's own state, especially the command line in sys.argv.
A module is one file, a package is a folder of modules with __init__.py, and the __name__ guard keeps test code out of imports.
Regular expressions trade readability for compact power; compile the pattern once and use raw strings so backslashes reach re unchanged.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are judged on a correct definition plus a complete, runnable program with its expected output, so keep clause order, file modes and library call signatures exact.

bank.q: Explain the four clauses of Python's exception-handling statement — try, except, else and finally — with a program that divides two numbers typed by the user. State the exact order in which the clauses run.
outline: Syntax and purpose of each clause
Order: try runs; on a matching exception the except body runs; else runs only if no exception; finally always runs
Division example catching ZeroDivisionError and ValueError from int()
Several except clauses are tested top to bottom, so put specific classes first
finally also runs when the try leaves through return or break

bank.q: Name the main built-in exception categories in Python and give one situation that triggers each. Show how to raise an exception deliberately and how to define and use your own exception class.
outline: BaseException at the top, Exception as the normal base for user errors
ArithmeticError, ZeroDivisionError, OverflowError
LookupError, IndexError, KeyError
ValueError and TypeError and how they differ
OSError family, FileNotFoundError, PermissionError
raise ValueError("negative amount") and re-raising with a bare raise
class InsufficientBalance(Exception) with __init__ calling super().__init__(message)
except InsufficientBalance as e: reading the message

bank.q: Explain the file object, the file pointer and the common mode strings of open(). Give the effect of each mode on an existing file and on a missing file.
outline: open() returns a file object; close() releases it
'r' read, error if missing; 'w' create or truncate; 'a' create or append; 'x' exclusive create
'b' binary and '+' read-write combinations
Pointer starts at 0 in 'r', at end in 'a'; tell() reports it, seek() moves it
read(), readline(), readlines(), write(), writelines()
with open(...) as f: closes automatically even on exception
Text mode decodes using an encoding; binary mode returns bytes

bank.q: What is a delimited text file? Explain the difference between CSV and tab-separated files, and show how the csv module reads and writes rows with reader, writer and DictReader.
outline: A table stored as plain text: one record per line, fields separated by a delimiter
Comma for CSV, tab for TSV; quoting when a field itself contains the delimiter
csv.reader yields a list of strings per line; csv.writer writes a list as one line
newline='' when opening for the csv module
DictReader and DictWriter map field names to column headers
Numbers arrive as strings and need int() or float()

bank.q: Explain the os and sys modules. List the functions used for creating, listing, renaming and removing directories, and explain sys.argv, sys.path and sys.exit().
outline: os.getcwd, os.chdir, os.listdir, os.mkdir, os.makedirs, os.rmdir, os.remove, os.rename
os.walk yields (dirpath, dirnames, filenames) for a whole tree
os.path.join, exists, isfile, isdir, getsize, splitext
sys.argv is the command line as a list; argv[0] is the script name
sys.path is the module search path; sys.exit(code) ends the program with a status
Portability: use os.path.join instead of writing slashes by hand

bank.q: Distinguish a module from a package. Explain how import finds a module, what __init__.py does, and why the __name__ == "__main__" guard is written.
outline: A module is one .py file; a package is a folder of modules with __init__.py
import math, from math import sqrt, import numpy as np
Search order: built-ins, then folders on sys.path including the script's folder
__init__.py marks the folder as a package and may run setup code
Dotted import: from college.results import topper
__name__ is "__main__" when run directly, the module name when imported
Guard keeps demo or test code out of the import path

bank.q: Explain regular expressions and the functions of the re module: search, match, findall, finditer, sub and split. Describe the meaning of the common metacharacters.
outline: A pattern language over strings; re compiles it into a pattern object
Metacharacters: . ^ $ * + ? {m,n} [] | () \d \w \s and their negations
Greedy versus non-greedy quantifiers
match anchors at the start, search scans anywhere, fullmatch requires the whole string
findall returns strings or tuples, finditer returns match objects with group()
sub for replacement, split for tokenising
Use raw strings r"\d+" so backslashes are not eaten

bank.q: A text file numbers.txt holds one number per line, but a few lines are corrupted. Write a program that reads every line, prints the average of the valid numbers, reports each bad line with its line number, and always prints "done" at the end.
outline: with open(...) for guaranteed close
Loop over the file object line by line with enumerate for line numbers
try: float(line); except ValueError: print the line number and skip
else clause to add to the total only on success
finally (or code after the loop) to print "done"
Handle FileNotFoundError around the open
Division by zero guard when no valid number was found

bank.q: Write a program for a wallet that stores a balance. Define an exception class InsufficientBalanceError carrying the shortfall. On withdrawal, raise it when the amount exceeds the balance, catch it in the caller and print the shortfall.
outline: class InsufficientBalanceError(Exception) with __init__ storing shortfall and calling super().__init__
withdraw method checks amount > balance and raises with a message
Caller uses try/except InsufficientBalanceError as e
Printing e and e.shortfall
Also catch ValueError for a negative or non-numeric amount
Balance unchanged after a failed withdrawal

bank.q: A file students.csv has the columns roll, name, marks. Write a program that reads it with the csv module, prints the topper's name and marks, and writes result.csv with an extra column PASS or FAIL at 40 marks.
outline: Open with newline='' in both directions
csv.DictReader for named columns, or reader plus int(row[2])
Track maximum marks while looping; convert marks with int()
csv.DictWriter with fieldnames and writeheader()
Conditional field for PASS/FAIL
Correct handling of a file with a header row only

bank.q: Write a script that takes a folder path as sys.argv[1] and prints every .py file under it, with its size in bytes and its path relative to the starting folder. Print a message if the argument is missing or the folder does not exist.
outline: Check len(sys.argv) and print a usage line, then sys.exit(1)
os.path.isdir check before walking
os.walk over the tree, filtering names with endswith('.py')
os.path.getsize and os.path.join for full paths
os.path.relpath for the relative path
sys.exit with a non-zero status on error

bank.q: Using the re module, write a program that validates Indian mobile numbers (ten digits starting with 6 to 9) and simple email addresses, and extracts all dates written as dd-mm-yyyy from a block of text.
outline: Pattern r"^[6-9]\d{9}$" with fullmatch for whole-string validation
Email pattern with characters before @, a domain and a dot plus letters
findall with groups for day, month, year
compile once, reuse the pattern object
Explain why anchors matter and why a raw string is used
Report each match or a clear invalid message

bank.q: Compare the two styles of guarding against errors — checking conditions before acting, and catching exceptions after acting. Discuss which Python style is preferred for file and network work, and evaluate the risks of an empty except clause and of a finally block that returns a value.
outline: Check-first style: test os.path.exists then open; cost of a second call and a race with other programs
Catch-after style: attempt the operation, handle the specific failure
Python idiom favours catching specific exceptions for input/output
except: pass hides real bugs including KeyboardInterrupt; catch named classes only
A return inside finally replaces any earlier return or exception, so avoid it
finally is for cleanup such as close, not for decisions
Conclusion: name the exception, keep the try block small

bank.q: A shop keeps transactions.csv with the columns date, upi_id, amount, where some rows have bad dates and non-numeric amounts. Design a program that validates and cleans the file, writes a clean CSV plus an error log, and is organised as a package with separate modules for validation and file input/output. Justify each design choice.
outline: Package layout: shop/__init__.py, shop/io_utils.py, shop/validate.py, main.py
Regular expression or datetime.strptime for the date, float() inside try for the amount
One user-defined exception such as InvalidRow carrying the line number
csv.DictReader over the input, csv.writer to the clean file, plain text log for rejects
with open for each file so every handle closes on error
__name__ guard in main.py and only function definitions in the helper modules
Trade-off: validating every row costs time but keeps bad data out of reports
Conclusion: separate reading, validating and writing so each part can be tested alone

glossary.def: An object created at run time that represents an error and interrupts the normal flow of statements.
The statements Python attempts first, with handlers attached for the errors they may raise.
A handler naming an exception class that runs when that class, or a subclass of it, is raised in the try.
The optional block of a try statement that runs only when no exception occurred.
The optional block of a try statement that always runs, used for cleanup.
The statement that throws an exception object to the nearest enclosing handler.
The tree of exception classes with BaseException at the root and Exception as the usual base for program errors.
A predefined exception class such as ValueError, IndexError or FileNotFoundError.
A class you write as a subclass of Exception to name and carry information about your own error.
The report Python prints showing the call stack and the line where an uncaught exception was raised.
The handle returned by open() through which a program reads from or writes to a file.
The current byte or character position in an open file, moved by seek() and read by tell().
The argument to open() that selects reading, writing, appending, binary or update behaviour.
An object usable in a with statement that performs setup on entry and cleanup on exit, such as an open file.
The character separating fields on one line of a formatted file.
Comma-separated values, a plain-text table format with one record per line.
A named set of formatting rules in the csv module, such as excel or excel-tab, controlling delimiter and quoting.
The standard library module providing directory operations and portable path helpers.
The standard library module exposing interpreter state such as argv, path, stdin, stdout and exit().
A single .py file whose names can be brought into another program with import.
A directory of modules containing an __init__.py file, imported under one dotted name.
The file that marks a directory as a package and runs when the package is first imported.
A module-level string equal to "__main__" when the file is run directly, otherwise the module's own name.
A pattern language describing a set of strings, used for matching, searching and replacing text.
A string written as r"..." in which backslashes are kept literally, useful for regex patterns and Windows paths.
The standard library module offering compile, match, search, findall, sub and split for regular expressions.
